approaches.name: BFS from the source
approaches.idea: Build adjacency lists and run a BFS from `source`; the answer is whether `destination` gets visited.
steps: Build the adjacency lists for the undirected edges.
BFS from `source`, marking visited nodes; stop early if `destination` is reached.
Return whether `destination` was visited.
approaches.why: Each node and edge is processed at most once.

approaches.name: Union–Find
approaches.idea: Union the two ends of every edge; afterwards, two nodes are connected exactly when they have the same root.
steps: Initialise `parent[i] = i`.
For each edge, union its endpoints (with path compression and union by size).
Return `find(source) == find(destination)`.
approaches.why: E unions and two finds, each nearly O(1). No adjacency lists are built, so it is light on memory.

redundant-connection.pattern: Union–Find: the first edge whose ends are already connected closes the cycle

approaches.name: Before adding each edge, search for an existing path
approaches.idea: Add edges one at a time. Before adding `[u, v]`, DFS in the graph built so far; if `u` already reaches `v`, this edge closes the cycle.
steps: Start with an empty graph.
For each edge `[u, v]`: if `u` can already reach `v` (DFS), return this edge.
Otherwise add the edge to the graph.
approaches.why: n edges, each followed by an O(n) search. With exactly one extra edge, the first edge that closes a cycle is the last cycle edge in the input, as required.

approaches.name: Union–Find
approaches.idea: Process edges in order, unioning their endpoints. The first edge whose endpoints already share a root would create a cycle — that is the redundant edge.
steps: Initialise `parent[i] = i` for nodes 1..n.
For each edge `[u, v]`: if `find(u) == find(v)`, return the edge.
Otherwise union them.
approaches.why: n near-constant union/find operations. As above, the first cycle-closing edge is the last cycle edge in the input order.

satisfiability-of-equality-equations.pattern: Union–Find: apply all equalities first, then check the inequalities

approaches.name: Graph of equalities and connected components
approaches.idea: Variables joined by `==` must share a value: they form connected components. An inequality `a != b` is impossible exactly when `a` and `b` are in the same component.
steps: Build an undirected graph on 26 letters with an edge for each `==`.
Label each letter with its component using DFS.
For each `!=` equation, return false if both letters have the same label. Otherwise return true.
approaches.why: n equations, and the graph has only 26 nodes, so the DFS is constant work. The edges stored are at most n, but the 26-node labelling is O(1).

approaches.name: Union–Find over 26 letters
approaches.idea: Two passes: first union the letters of every `==`, then check that no `!=` joins two letters with the same root. Doing all equalities first matters, because an equality later in the list can merge groups.
steps: Initialise `parent` for 26 letters.
Pass 1: for each `a==b`, union `a` and `b`.
Pass 2: for each `a!=b`, if `find(a) == find(b)`, return false.
Return true.
approaches.why: Two passes over the n equations with near-constant finds on a 26-element array.

smallest-string-with-swaps.pattern: Connected components of indices; sort the letters inside each component

approaches.name: DFS components, then sort each one
approaches.idea: Swaps along connected pairs can produce any arrangement of the letters within a connected group of indices. So, per group, put its letters in sorted order into its indices in sorted order.
steps: Build a graph on indices with an edge per pair.
For each unvisited index, collect its component with an iterative DFS.
Sort the component's indices and its letters; write the smallest letter at the smallest index, and so on.
Return the new string.
approaches.why: Finding components is O(n + p) for p pairs; sorting all components together costs O(n log n). The graph takes O(n + p).

approaches.name: Union–Find, then counting sort per group
approaches.idea: Union the indices of every pair. Then count the letters in each group (26 counters per root) and fill the indices from left to right with each group's smallest remaining letter.
steps: Union every pair.
For each index, add its letter to the counts of its root.
Walk indices from left to right; for index `i` with root `r`, write the smallest letter whose count in `r` is still positive, and decrease that count.
approaches.why: Union–Find handles the pairs; counting replaces sorting. Scanning for the smallest letter takes at most 26 steps per index.

approaches.name: Union–Find over account indices
approaches.idea: Map each email to the first account that listed it. When another account lists the same email, union the two accounts. Each final group of accounts is one person; collect its emails into a sorted set.
steps: For each account `i` and each of its emails: if the email was seen in account `j`, union `i` and `j`; otherwise record `owner[email] = i`.
For each email, add it to the set of `find(owner[email])`.
For each root, output `[name, ...sorted emails]`.
approaches.why: E is the total number of emails. Unions are near-constant; sorting each person's emails dominates.

approaches.name: DFS over an email graph
approaches.idea: Link every email of an account to the account's first email. Each connected component of this graph is one person; collect it with a DFS.
steps: For each account, connect its first email to each of its other emails (both ways) and remember each email's name.
DFS from every unvisited email to collect its component.
Sort the component and prepend the name.
approaches.why: The graph has E nodes and fewer than E edges; DFS is linear, and sorting each component dominates.

min-cost-to-connect-all-points.pattern: Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal with Union–Find, or Prim)

approaches.name: Kruskal: sort all edges, add those that join two components
approaches.idea: Consider every pair as an edge weighted by Manhattan distance. Take edges from cheapest to most expensive, keeping an edge only if it connects two different components (Union–Find). After n − 1 edges, all points are connected at minimum cost.
steps: Generate all n(n − 1)/2 edges with their costs and sort them.
For each edge in order, if its endpoints are in different sets, union them and add the cost.
Stop after n − 1 edges; return the total.
approaches.why: There are about n²/2 = 5·10⁵ edges to store and sort. Correct by the cut property: the cheapest edge leaving any component is in some MST.

approaches.name: Prim's algorithm on the dense graph
approaches.idea: Grow the tree from point 0. Keep, for every point outside the tree, the cheapest connection to any point inside it. Repeatedly add the outside point with the cheapest connection and update the others from it. With all pairs as edges, a plain array beats a heap.
steps: Set `dist[i] = ∞` for all points, `dist[0] = 0`.
Repeat n times: pick the point `u` not in the tree with the smallest `dist`; add it and add `dist[u]` to the total.
For every point `v` not in the tree, set `dist[v] = min(dist[v], cost(u, v))`.
Return the total.
approaches.why: n rounds of O(n) scanning and updating; no edge list is ever built. For a complete graph this matches the number of edges, so it is optimal.

regions-cut-by-slashes.pattern: Split each cell into pieces and count connected components (Union–Find or flood fill)

approaches.name: Draw the grid at 3× size and flood fill
approaches.idea: Scale each cell up to a 3 × 3 block of pixels and draw `/` or `\` as a diagonal of blocked pixels. The regions are then ordinary connected components of free pixels, counted with a flood fill.
steps: Make a `3n × 3n` pixel grid. For `/` in cell `(r, c)`, block pixels `(3r + k, 3c + 2 − k)`; for `\`, block `(3r + k, 3c + k)`, for `k = 0..2`.
Count connected groups of free pixels with BFS (4 directions).
approaches.why: 9n² pixels are filled and searched once. Two pixels per cell side are needed so that regions do not leak through the corners of a diagonal — 3× scaling is the smallest that works.

approaches.name: Union–Find over four triangles per cell
approaches.idea: Split each cell into four triangles: top (0), right (1), bottom (2), left (3). A space joins all four; `/` joins top–left and right–bottom; `\` joins top–right and bottom–left. Neighbouring cells always join along their shared edge. The number of distinct sets is the number of regions.
steps: Create 4n² triangles in a Union–Find; `regions` starts at 4n² and drops by one per successful union.
Inside each cell, union according to its character.
Union the cell's bottom with the top of the cell below, and its right with the left of the cell to the right.
Return `regions`.
approaches.why: A constant number of unions per cell. It uses 4n² entries instead of 9n² pixels, and needs no flood fill.

largest-component-size-by-common-factor.pattern: Union–Find through prime factors (numbers sharing a prime join the same set)

approaches.name: Union every pair with a common factor
approaches.idea: Check every pair of numbers with gcd; if it is greater than 1, union them. Then report the largest set.
steps: For every pair `i < j`, if `gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1`, union `i` and `j`.
Count the members of each root and return the largest count.
approaches.why: n²/2 gcd computations of O(log M) each: 2·10⁸ gcds for n = 2·10⁴.

approaches.name: Union each number with its prime factors
approaches.idea: Two numbers share a factor > 1 exactly when they share a prime factor. Put numbers and primes in one Union–Find (indexed by value): union each number with each of its prime factors. Numbers sharing a prime end up together without ever comparing pairs.
steps: Create a Union–Find over values `0 .. max(nums)`.
For each number, factor it by trial division up to its square root; union the number with every prime factor found (and with the leftover factor if it is greater than 1).
Count how many of the input numbers share each root; return the largest count.
approaches.why: Trial division takes at most √M ≈ 316 steps per number (M = 10⁵), with near-constant unions. The Union–Find covers every value up to M.

approaches.name: DFS from node 0
approaches.idea: A tree has exactly n − 1 edges. With that many edges, it is a tree exactly when one DFS from node 0 reaches every node.
steps: If `edges.length != n − 1`, return `false`.
Build an adjacency list and DFS (or BFS) from node 0, marking visited nodes.
Return whether all `n` nodes were visited.
approaches.why: With n − 1 edges, "connected" and "acyclic" are equivalent, so a reachability check is enough. The adjacency list stores every edge twice.

approaches.name: Union-find cycle check
approaches.idea: With exactly n − 1 edges, merge the endpoints of each edge. If an edge joins two nodes that are already in the same set, it closes a cycle.
steps: If `edges.length != n − 1`, return `false`.
Start with each node as its own set. For each edge, find both roots.
If the roots are equal, return `false`; otherwise merge them. Return `true` at the end.
approaches.why: No adjacency list is needed, and path compression keeps each find nearly constant. n − 1 edges with no cycle always connect all n nodes, so no separate connectivity check is required.

number-of-connected-components-in-an-und.pattern: Count components with DFS starts, or union-find merges

approaches.name: DFS from every unvisited node
approaches.idea: Each time you start a search from a node that has not been visited, you discover one new component.
steps: Build an adjacency list.
For each node `0..n − 1` not yet visited: increase the count and DFS from it, marking everything reachable.
Return the count.
approaches.why: Every node and edge is processed once. The adjacency list and visited array take linear space.

approaches.name: Union-find
approaches.idea: Start with n separate components. Every edge that joins two different sets merges them and removes one component.
steps: Initialise `parent[i] = i` and `comps = n`.
For each edge, find both roots; if they differ, link them and decrement `comps`.
Return `comps`.
approaches.why: No adjacency list is needed and each union is nearly constant time with path compression. It also works when edges arrive one at a time, where DFS would have to start over.

find-critical-and-pseudo-critical-edges-.pattern: Kruskal's MST re-run with one edge excluded or forced

approaches.name: Re-sort for every Kruskal run
approaches.idea: Compute the best MST weight. For each edge, build an MST without it (heavier or disconnected → critical); otherwise build one that starts with it (same weight → pseudo-critical).
steps: `mst(skip, force)`: copy and sort the edges by weight, add `force` first if given, then add every non-skipped edge that joins two different sets; return the weight, or ∞ if fewer than n − 1 edges were used.
`best = mst(none, none)`.
For each edge `i`: if `mst(i, none) > best` it is critical; else if `mst(none, i) == best` it is pseudo-critical.
approaches.why: About 2E Kruskal runs, each sorting the edges again. With E ≤ 200 that is fast, but sorting once outside the loop is an easy win.

approaches.name: Sort once, then 2E union-find passes
approaches.idea: The same two tests per edge, but the edges are sorted a single time and every Kruskal run just walks that order with a fresh union-find.
steps: Sort edge indices by weight once.
`mst(skip, force)` walks the sorted order with a new union-find (adding `force` first) and returns the weight or ∞.
Classify each edge exactly as before: heavier without it → critical; optimal when forced → pseudo-critical.
approaches.why: Each run is a single linear pass, so the total is about 2E passes of E near-constant steps. Why forcing works: if some MST contains edge i, Kruskal with i added first still finds an MST of the best weight; if none does, the forced tree must be heavier.

approaches.name: Pairwise gcd graph + BFS
approaches.idea: Connect every pair of indices whose values have gcd greater than 1, then check that one BFS reaches every index.
steps: If there is one element, return `true`.
BFS from index 0: for the current index, scan every unvisited index `j` and visit it if `gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1`.
Return whether all indices were visited.
approaches.why: Each of up to n popped indices scans all others, with an O(log V) gcd each. For 10⁵ numbers that is about 10¹⁰ gcd calls, so it times out on the large test.

approaches.name: Sieve + union by prime factor
approaches.idea: Two values share a gcd above 1 exactly when they share a prime. Give every prime its own union-find node and union each index with the primes that divide its value.
steps: Handle n = 1 (true) and any value 1 when n > 1 (false: 1 shares no prime with anything).
Build a smallest-prime-factor table up to max(nums) with a sieve.
Union index `i` with node `n + p` for every distinct prime `p` of `nums[i]`, then check that all indices share one root.
approaches.time: O(V log log V + n log V)
approaches.why: V = max(nums). The sieve is near-linear, and each value has at most about 6 distinct primes under 10⁵, found in O(log V) divisions using the table. Prime nodes act as hubs, so the graph never needs the O(n²) pairwise edges.
